[ · #27] Why my nose gets all tickly when flowers come?
[ · #28] That happens because, in spring, many plants and trees make something very tiny called *pollen*. Pollen is like tiny yellow dust that flowers and trees release into the air so new plants can grow. You can’t always see it, but it floats around outside, especially on warm, windy days.

When you breathe in pollen, the inside of your nose and sometimes your eyes think it’s a ‘bad’ thing, even though pollen isn’t dangerous. Your body’s helper system, called the *immune system*, gets a little too worried. It sends out a signal by making extra mucus (the runny stuff in your nose) and making you sneeze to try to push the pollen away. That sneezy, itchy, tickly feeling is your body’s way of protecting itself.

Different times of year have different levels of pollen. Spring has a lot, because so many flowers, grasses, and trees are waking up after winter. If you notice it happens every time flowers start blooming, that’s because there’s more pollen in the air then. Staying inside on very windy, flowery days or washing your hands and face after playing outside can sometimes help you feel better. [ · #29] Yes, please! How can I check if the pollen is high?

Usually, pollen levels are highest in the morning and on warm, windy days. So, if you see that the pollen count is high, you can plan to play outside later in the afternoon or choose days when it’s cooler or raining, which washes the pollen out of the air. This way, you can enjoy being outside while keeping your nose from getting too tickly!

[ · #246] Why my skin not itchy now when it’s dry outside?
[ · #247] That’s a really good question, Mateo! Our skin has a special outer layer that works a bit like a shield, keeping water inside and keeping things from the outside from bothering us. When it’s dry outside, the air tries to pull the water out of our skin faster, and that can sometimes make it feel itchy.

But sometimes, our skin learns to stay stronger against that dryness. This can happen because your body might be making more of its natural protective oils, or maybe you’ve been using lotion more often, eating healthy foods, or drinking enough water to keep your skin hydrated from the inside.

Another possible reason is that little changes in your daily life—like wearing the right kind of clothes, bathing with water that’s not too hot, or having the heater or air in your house adjusted—can give your skin more help so it doesn’t dry out quickly. Even small things, like spending less time in very windy places or playing outside at different times of day, can change how your skin feels.

And for some kids, as they get a bit older, their skin can become less sensitive to certain weather, so dry days don’t cause as much itching anymore. So it’s like your skin has gotten better at holding on to its own comfort, even when the air isn’t holding much water.
